title: Légal's Trap
subtitle: Philidor Defense
summary: White offers the queen to expose a hidden mating net, punishing Black for grabbing material instead of finishing development.

rootAnnotations.title: Named after Sire de Légal
rootAnnotations.body: This trap is named for the 18th-century French master Sire de Légal, said to have sprung it on an overconfident opponent. It shows that a pin is only as strong as what's actually behind the pinned piece.

annotations.title: A pin with nothing behind it
annotations.body: This looks like a standard pin of the knight to the queen, but the black king is on e8, not on the d1-h5 diagonal. It is only a relative pin — the knight is free to move if something bigger is at stake.

annotations.title: Offering the queen
annotations.body: White ignores the 'pin' and grabs a pawn, apparently hanging the queen to Bxd1. But the real point is a forced mate — the queen is worth less than what follows it.

annotations.title: The greedy capture
annotations.body: Taking the queen looks winning, but it walks straight into a forced mate. Black should have recaptured the knight instead of grabbing material — see the alternative line.

annotations.title: The safe, correct choice
annotations.body: Simply recapturing the knight is right. After 6.Qxg4 White has only won a pawn for the trouble — a small, normal edge instead of a forced loss.

annotations.title: Dragging the king out
annotations.body: With the queen gone, White's remaining pieces do the real work. This check forces the king into the open, since nothing can capture or block on f7.

annotations.title: The only legal move
annotations.body: Kxf7 runs into the knight on e5, which guards f7; that same knight also covers d7, and f8 is occupied by Black's own bishop. Ke7 is forced.

annotations.title: The mating net
annotations.body: The knight from c3 delivers mate: it covers e7, d7, and f6, the bishop on f7 covers e6 and e8, and Black's own queen and bishop block the rest. There is no escape.
